turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I’m here because... honestly, for months now I’ve been trying to get people to understand what my husband’s family is doing. They're quietly messing with our money and our good name. Like, I work as a billing clerk, and lately these little billing errors just keep showing up out of nowhere. It's funny, actually, because it reminds me of when we switched our computer system back in 2018, and my old supervisor Brenda—she retired and moved down to Florida, somewhere near Tampa, I think, or maybe Clearwater—she always hated that new software. She said it was too sensitive. 

But this isn't a computer glitch. And it's not just at work, it's church too. People there are suddenly acting funny toward me. Just last Sunday I was talking about the upcoming bake sale, and I always make my grandmother's lemon pound cake for it. She used to grow her own lemons, right in her backyard, the absolute biggest lemons you've ever seen... but anyway, what I'm saying is, no matter what records anyone pulls up or what they try to tell me, I know it all ties back to his family. They're the ones behind it.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that her husband's family is sabotaging her finances and reputation, maintaining this conviction regardless of any contradictory records or evidence.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality, as she frequently wanders off-topic into unrelated details about her former supervisor moving to Florida and her grandmother's lemon tree before returning to her main point.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been hearing voices when no one else is there?
turns.patient_response: Voices? No, I don't hear anything like that. I mean, my hearing is really sharp, though. I can hear the hum of the refrigerator from all the way in the living room. It’s a Whirlpool, actually. We bought it on sale at Sears right before they closed the one over at the Westside mall. That mall used to be so nice back in the day, you know? They had this amazing soft pretzel stand right by the food court, and at Christmas, they’d put up a tree that went all the way up to the skylight. I took my niece there to see Santa once when she was maybe four or five. She had on this little red velvet dress with white tights that got a chocolate stain on them before we even made it to the line... but, anyway, no, I don't hear people talking when nobody is there. Just regular house noises.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, wandering from the hum of a refrigerator to a closed mall, a pretzel stand, and a detailed memory of their niece before finally returning to the question.

turns.doctor_question: Have there been times when you felt unusually high, energetic, or full of energy for days at a time?
turns.patient_response: Unusually high or energetic? No, I don't think so. I've always been pretty steady. I mean, I have to be, with my job. Working as a billing clerk, you sit a lot. You really have to make sure you get up and stretch, otherwise your lower back just completely locks up. My sister-in-law, the one who married my brother David, she bought me one of those ergonomic cushions for my desk chair last Christmas. It’s got this memory foam in it that's supposed to mold to your shape. She got it off one of those home shopping channels, I think. She watches QVC all day long, buying the most ridiculous things. Last month she bought this set of copper pots that she swore were non-stick, but the very first time she tried to make scrambled eggs, they stuck right to the bottom. It took her three days of soaking just to get it clean. But anyway, no, I haven't had any days where I felt like I was full of energy or anything like that. Just my normal routine.

turns.doctor_question: If someone shows you clear proof that your husband’s family is not involved, are you able to accept that?
turns.patient_response:
Clear proof? Well... what kind of proof are we talking about? Because I've seen the records they pull up, and I know how easy it is to doctor a spreadsheet or a bank statement. People think computers are foolproof, but they aren't. My nephew, the one who just started his freshman year at State—he's studying computer science, actually. He built his own computer in his bedroom from parts he ordered online. It took up his whole desk, and it had these glowing blue lights inside the case. His mother was furious because he spent his entire summer job savings on it instead of saving for a car. She drives this old Honda Civic that’s been making a terrible rattling noise under the hood, but she refuses to take it to the mechanic because she says they always try to upsell her on air filters and wiper blades... 

But anyway, what I'm saying is, I wouldn't believe their "proof." I know what I know. For months I've been trying to get people to understand that his family is quietly messing with our money and our good name. The billing errors at work, the way the ladies at church are suddenly acting so funny toward me... no matter what piece of paper someone tries to show me, I know it all ties back to them. They're doing it, and I'm not going to just pretend they aren't because someone hands me a fake printout.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient demonstrates a fixed belief that her husband's family is sabotaging her, explicitly stating she would reject any contradictory evidence or 'proof' as being faked.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech by going off on a long, irrelevant tangent about her nephew's computer and his mother's car before returning to the main topic.

turns.doctor_question: Do people ever tell you that your thoughts or the way you talk jump around or are hard to follow?
turns.patient_response: Jump around? No, nobody's ever said that to me. I think I'm pretty clear when I speak. You have to be clear when you work in billing. If you get one number wrong, or explain a code poorly, the whole insurance claim gets kicked back. And you know how insurance companies are. They'll use any excuse to deny a claim. My cousin Brenda, she had this terrible time with her insurance last year when she needed that knee surgery. She tore her meniscus slipping on the ice in her driveway. It was one of those freak ice storms we got in February, remember? The whole city basically shut down for two days. The salt trucks didn't even make it to her neighborhood until the second afternoon. She was trying to walk down to get the mail because she was waiting for a birthday card from her son who lives out in Arizona. He moved out there for the dry heat, says it helps his allergies. But anyway, no, people don't tell me I'm hard to follow. I just tell things exactly how they happen.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly denies that their thoughts jump around or that people find their speech hard to follow.

turns.doctor_question: Have you found yourself losing interest in seeing people or doing things you usually enjoy?
turns.patient_response: Losing interest? No, I don't think so. I mean, I still like doing the things I usually do. Like my garden, I try to keep up with the flower beds out front. Mostly marigolds and some petunias. Though I will say, the slugs have been absolutely terrible this year. Have you noticed that? It's because we had such a wet spring. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he's lived next door for thirty years, he told me to put out little shallow dishes of beer to catch them. He says they're attracted to the yeast or something and they just crawl right in and drown. He buys the cheapest beer he can find at the discount liquor store over on 4th Street. The one next to that old dry cleaner that closed down? I used to take my winter coats there, but the last time I did, they lost the belt to my navy trench coat and refused to pay for it. The owner was this very stubborn man who insisted I brought it in without a belt. Why would I bring a trench coat in without a belt? It completely ruins the silhouette. But anyway, I still enjoy my garden and things like that. I just haven't been as social lately, but that's only because of everything going on with his family, you know? You have to be careful who you spend time with.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering off-topic from gardening to slugs, a neighbor, a liquor store, and a dry cleaner dispute before returning to the original point.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient explicitly denies losing interest in activities they usually enjoy, stating they still like doing their usual things like gardening.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever felt that other people could read your thoughts?
turns.patient_response: Read my thoughts? No, I don't think anyone can do that. That sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. My husband loves those kinds of movies, the ones with aliens and mind readers and spaceships. He used to make me watch them with him when we first got married. We had this huge, heavy tube TV back then, the kind that took two people just to lift it onto the stand. The picture quality was terrible compared to what we have now, but we didn't know any better. We'd rent VHS tapes from Blockbuster on Friday nights. Remember Blockbuster? It's such a shame they all closed down. I used to love walking down the aisles, looking at all the covers. The smell of the popcorn they sold by the register... I bought a box of microwave popcorn last week, the extra butter kind, but it just doesn't taste the same. I think they changed the oil they use or something. The bag says "new and improved flavor," but whenever a company says that, it usually just means they found a cheaper way to make it. It's like the brand of coffee I used to buy for the office breakroom. One day the packaging changed, and suddenly it tasted like burnt toast. I had to switch us to a different brand, which caused a whole fuss with the accounting department because it cost fifty cents more a can. But anyway, no, nobody can read my thoughts. I just keep them to myself, especially with everything his family is doing. You have to keep your thoughts private these days.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and derailment, wandering through loosely connected topics like old TVs, Blockbuster, popcorn, and coffee before finally returning to the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe your husband’s family has any special powers or unusual ways of controlling events that other people wouldn’t normally be able to do?
turns.patient_response: Special powers? No, no, they don't have magic powers or anything like that. That's ridiculous. They're just very... manipulative. They know how to pull strings. Speaking of pulling strings, did you know I used to knit? I made this beautiful cable-knit sweater for my husband for our fifth anniversary. It took me months. I had to special order the yarn from a little shop up in Maine because I wanted this specific heather gray color. The woman who ran the shop, Mrs. Higgins, she was so sweet. She used to send a little handwritten note with every order and a complimentary stitch marker. They were always shaped like little sheep. I had quite a collection of them by the time she retired and closed the shop. It's so hard to find good quality wool these days without spending a fortune. Everything in the craft stores now is acrylic. It just doesn't breathe the same way, you know? You put on an acrylic sweater and five minutes later you're sweating, but you're still cold. It makes no sense. I tried to explain that to my sister when she started making baby blankets, but she just wanted something you could throw in the washer. But no, his family doesn't have special powers. They're just very good at getting people to do what they want, normal things, just... twisted.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a lengthy, verbose response filled with unnecessary details about knitting and yarn.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient demonstrates derailment and loose associations, shifting abruptly from the phrase 'pull strings' to a long, unrelated tangent about knitting.

turns.doctor_question: Before all of this started, have you generally tended to distrust other people and suspect they were trying to harm or deceive you?
turns.patient_response: Distrust people? Oh, no, not at all. I've always been a very trusting person. Too trusting, maybe. I used to be the one at the office who would leave my purse right out on my desk when I went to the restroom. I mean, we're all adults, right? We had this one woman, Brenda, who started in the billing department a few years ago. She was always borrowing things. A pen here, a stapler there. One time she borrowed my favorite mug—it was this ceramic one I got on a trip to Sedona, painted with these beautiful little desert flowers. The glaze was so vibrant. Anyway, she borrowed it for her tea and then left it in the sink for three days. I finally had to wash it myself. The water in our breakroom sink was always lukewarm, never hot enough to really get things clean, which I always thought was a health hazard. I brought it up to the building manager, this guy named Tom, who always wore these terrible clip-on ties. He said he'd look into the water heater, but he never did. He was always making excuses, saying the pipes were too old. But anyway, no, I've never been the suspicious type. I always try to see the good in people, until they give me a reason not to. It's just that now, with his family, they've given me plenty of reasons. But before that? No, I never thought people were out to get me.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and derailment, wandering extensively from the initial topic of trust to a coworker, a ceramic mug, breakroom plumbing, and a building manager's attire before finally returning to the point.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been convinced that your husband’s family is doing this for more than one month?
turns.patient_response: Oh, definitely more than a month. It's been going on for about nine months now. It all started right around the time we had that big blow-up over money and the holiday expectations. Holidays used to be so nice, you know? I used to bake these incredible gingerbread cookies from scratch. My grandmother gave me the recipe. She always insisted on using dark molasses, not the light kind, and you have to chill the dough overnight or it spreads too much in the oven. I had these antique copper cookie cutters shaped like little stars and reindeer. They were so hard to keep clean, though. Copper tarnishes so fast if you don't polish it. I used to buy this special cream polish from a hardware store downtown, but they closed last year to make room for another one of those fancy coffee shops. You can't even get a regular cup of drip coffee there anymore, it's all lattes and macchiatos and things you can't pronounce. And they charge six dollars for it! It's highway robbery. My husband used to drink his coffee black, just like his father did. His father was a very stern man, never smiled in pictures. We have this one photo of him from our wedding... but anyway, yes, it's been about nine months since they started all this nonsense with me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient confirms holding a fixed belief about her husband's family ('all this nonsense') that has persisted for nine months.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, wandering extensively through unrelated topics (cookies, copper polish, coffee shops) before returning to the original point.

turns.doctor_question: Have you felt that someone was controlling your actions or putting thoughts into your mind?
turns.patient_response: Controlling my actions? Putting thoughts in my head? No, no, I'm fully in control of myself. My thoughts are my own. I've always had a very strong mind, actually. My mother used to say I was too stubborn for my own good. She was always trying to get me to wear dresses when I was little, but I hated them. I only wanted to wear these corduroy overalls. They were navy blue with little brass buttons on the straps. I wore them until the knees completely wore out. You just can't find good corduroy anymore. Everything now is that thin, stretchy material that loses its shape after one wash. I bought a pair of pants last month from that department store at the mall—the one that used to be a Sears before they remodeled the whole wing. They put in a huge food court with this terrible lighting that gives you a headache if you sit there too long. I went there to get a pretzel, you know, the soft ones with the big grains of salt? But the line was a mile long, so I just left. Anyway, no, nobody is putting thoughts in my head. I know exactly what I'm doing and thinking. It's just his family that's the problem, not my own mind.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality and derailment, wandering from the topic of thought control to childhood overalls, department stores, food courts, and pretzels before finally returning to the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever feel that other people can hear your thoughts as you think them?
turns.patient_response: Hear my thoughts? Oh, goodness, no. That sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. Like that one with the aliens that came down in those big silver saucers—what was it called? The Day the Earth Stood Still? My husband loved those old black-and-white movies. We used to stay up late on Friday nights watching them on this tiny little Zenith television we had in our first apartment. It had the rabbit ear antennas, and you had to wrap aluminum foil around the tips just to get a clear picture of channel 4. We lived right near the airport back then, so every time a plane flew over, the screen would get all fuzzy and the sound would buzz. I tried wedging a piece of cardboard in the side to stop the rattling, but it never really worked. The cardboard came from a box of oranges my uncle sent us from Florida. He had a grove down there, Valencia oranges, I think. They were the sweetest oranges I've ever tasted, so much juice you had to eat them over the sink. But anyway, no, nobody can hear what I'm thinking. That's just silly. My thoughts are perfectly private.

turns.doctor_question: During these past nine months, have you had a period when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?
turns.patient_response: Depressed? No, I wouldn't say I've been depressed. I mean, it's stressful dealing with his family, obviously, but I haven't been sitting around crying all day or anything like that. I still go to work every day. I do billing at a dental office, you know. It keeps me busy. Too busy, sometimes. The new software they installed last month is just a nightmare. It's supposed to be "cloud-based," whatever that means, but it crashes every time I try to run the end-of-day reports. I told Dr. Henderson we should have just stuck with the old system. It was slow, sure, but at least I knew how to fix it when it froze. You just had to hit Control, Alt, Delete, and wait for the little hourglass icon to go away. Do you remember when computers used to have that hourglass? Now it's just that spinning blue circle. It makes me dizzy if I look at it too long. I actually had to get new glasses last year because I was getting such bad headaches from staring at the screen. I went to that optometrist over on Elm Street, the one with the green awning. He told me I have a slight astigmatism in my left eye. My sister has that too, but hers is much worse. She can't even drive at night because the headlights look like big starbursts to her. She used to drive this old Volvo station wagon, the kind that looked like a tank... but no, I haven't been depressed. Just frustrated with his family, that's all.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the topic of depression to work software, computer icons, glasses, and her sister's car.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies feeling depressed or spending the day crying.

turns.doctor_question: Since this began, have you had trouble keeping up with your work or daily responsibilities?
turns.patient_response: Trouble keeping up? No, no, I manage just fine. I still get up every morning, make my coffee, and go in to handle all my billing clerk duties at the dental office. I keep the house going, too. I even find time for my gardening and painting. I was just out in the garden yesterday evening, actually, trying to save my hydrangeas. The Japanese beetles have been absolutely terrible this year. They just skeletonize the leaves, you know? It's heartbreaking after you put so much work into them. I tried spraying them with that neem oil mixture my neighbor recommended. She swears by it, says it kept all the bugs off her prize-winning tomatoes last summer. She grows those big heirloom ones, the Cherokee Purples, I think they're called. They make the best BLT sandwiches if you toast the sourdough bread just right and use a really thick-cut bacon. My husband used to get this applewood smoked bacon from a butcher shop two towns over, but they closed down during the pandemic. Such a shame, it was a family-owned place, been there for three generations. The grandson was running it, but I guess he just couldn't keep the lights on... But anyway, my daily responsibilities are fine. The only real trouble I have is when I try to warn people about what my in-laws are doing. That's what takes up my energy, trying to make people understand what's going on with them. But the house and work? I'm completely on top of all that.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient mentions expending energy trying to warn people and make them understand what her in-laws are doing, indicating a persistent delusional belief.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from gardening to beetles, tomatoes, BLT sandwiches, and a closed butcher shop before returning to the topic.

turns.doctor_question: Has anyone at work, at home, or at church told you that the way you talk is hard for them to follow?
turns.patient_response: Hard to follow? Me? No, nobody's ever said that. I mean, I speak perfectly clearly. I was in the debate club in high school, you know. We went all the way to the state championships my senior year. Our topic was whether or not the voting age should be lowered, and I had to argue the affirmative side. I wore this awful navy blue suit my mother bought me from JCPenney. It had these huge shoulder pads that made me look like a linebacker. That was back when everyone was wearing those big shoulder pads, like on Dynasty or Dallas. My mom never missed an episode of Dallas. She had this huge crush on Patrick Duffy. She even bought a mug with his face on it at a garage sale once. It was a really nice garage sale, actually, over in the nice part of town by the golf course. I bought a set of vintage Pyrex mixing bowls there for practically nothing. The primary colors ones—red, yellow, green, and blue. The blue one is my favorite, I use it every time I make my grandmother's potato salad. The secret is to add a little bit of sweet pickle relish and a dash of paprika on top. It looks so pretty when you serve it at a picnic. We used to have picnics all the time down by the lake before they built those ugly new condos... But no, no one has ever told me I'm hard to follow. I think I'm very easy to understand.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly denies that anyone has ever told them their speech is hard to follow, stating they believe they speak perfectly clearly and are easy to understand.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever feel that outside forces are controlling your actions?
turns.patient_response: Controlling my actions? Like, making me move my arms or something? No, I'm the only one in control of what I do. I mean, my in-laws try to control my life with all their scheming, but they aren't physically controlling my body like a puppet. That sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. My husband loves those movies, the ones with the aliens and the spaceships. We went to see that new one last month, the one with the really loud sound effects. The theater was freezing, too. They always keep the air conditioning blasting in those places. I had to wear my heavy wool sweater, the gray one I knitted myself. It took me three months to finish that sweater because I kept messing up the cable stitch on the sleeves. Knitting is supposed to be relaxing, but sometimes it just makes me more tense. My aunt Martha taught me how to knit when I was ten. She lived in this tiny little house that always smelled like peppermint and mothballs. She had a cat named Barnaby who was missing half his left ear. He got into a fight with a raccoon, she said. Raccoons can be so vicious, you know. They get into the garbage cans and just make a huge mess. I had to buy those special bungee cords to keep the lids on our cans because the raccoons were having a feast every Tuesday night before trash day... But no, nobody is controlling my actions. I do what I want to do.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient mentions making careless mistakes by repeatedly messing up the cable stitch on her sweater.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits severe tangentiality, drifting from the topic of being controlled to sci-fi movies, a cold theater, knitting, her aunt, a cat, and raccoons before finally returning to the question.

turns.doctor_question: Has anyone ever told you that when you talk, you go off on tangents or lose track of the main point?
turns.patient_response:
Lose track of the main point? No, I don't think anyone has ever said that to me. I'm actually very good at keeping track of things. You really have to be in my line of work, you know? Doing all the billing at the dental office, if you lose track of even one little decimal point, it's a complete disaster. 

Just last Tuesday, I caught a huge error on an insurance claim for Mrs. Higgins' new crown. She got a gold crown on her back molar. You really don't see gold crowns as much anymore, do you? Everyone wants the porcelain ones now so they blend in with their real teeth. My uncle Arthur had a whole mouthful of gold teeth, though. He used to chew on ice cubes all the time, which is just terrible for your enamel. Dr. Evans is always telling our patients not to do that. He’s the senior partner at the practice. Well, he’s retiring next year, actually. He and his wife bought a condo down in Florida. Sarasota, I think. Or maybe it was Naples. 

My sister went to Sarasota for her honeymoon back in... oh, it must have been 1998. They stayed at this gorgeous resort right on the water, but it rained for four days straight. She was so furious. She spent almost the whole trip just sitting in the hotel lobby drinking overpriced coffee and reading paperback romance novels. She loves those Nora Roberts books. She has a whole big oak bookshelf dedicated to them in her guest room, the room with the yellow floral wallpaper. She put that wallpaper up herself, which is really hard to do without getting air bubbles in it... but anyway, no, nobody has ever told me I go off on tangents. I always get right to the point.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever believed that people were sending you special messages through the television, radio, or newspaper?
turns.patient_response:
Special messages? From the TV or the newspaper? No, I don't think so. I mean, the news is just the news, right? Though honestly, I barely watch the news anymore. It's just so depressing lately. Always about the economy or some terrible accident on the highway. 

We had a really bad accident near my house last winter. A semi-truck jackknifed on the overpass right when it started snowing. It was that really wet, heavy snow that just sticks to everything and brings down the power lines. We lost power for three whole days. I had to empty out my entire chest freezer because everything started to thaw. All that meat, just ruined. My husband had just bought a quarter of a cow from a local farmer, too. It was grass-fed beef, which is supposed to be so much better for you, but it's terribly expensive. We had to throw out at least thirty pounds of ground beef and these beautiful ribeye steaks. 

I tried to save some of it by cooking it on the little camping stove we have in the garage, but you can only eat so many hamburgers in one day, you know? That camping stove is older than my kids. We bought it at a sporting goods store that went out of business years ago. They had a huge liquidation sale, and we got it for half price. My husband loves a good bargain. He’ll drive twenty miles out of his way just to save five cents a gallon on gas. I keep telling him he's probably burning more gas just driving there, but he won't listen. He’s stubborn like that. His whole family is stubborn. His sister once refused to speak to him for a year because of an argument over a game of Monopoly... but anyway, no, I don't get any special messages from the TV or anything. Just the regular programs.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies believing that special messages are being sent to them through the TV or newspaper.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, wandering through a long chain of loosely related topics (accident, snow, freezer, camping stove, husband's stubbornness) before returning to the original question.
